paragraphs: A young disciple came to his teacher and announced that he wanted religion. The old master just looked at him and smiled, saying nothing. The young man kept turning up, day after day, repeating the same thing. But the old man understood far better than the youth what that wish actually meant.

One scorching day, the teacher invited the young man to come down to the river with him for a dip. The disciple jumped in, and the master followed. Then, without warning, he pushed the young man under and held him there. The disciple thrashed and fought. After a while the teacher let him up and asked: what did you want most when you were down there? 'A breath of air,' gasped the disciple.

Do you want God like that? asked the master. If you do, you will find Him in an instant. Without that kind of thirst, he said, no amount of clever thinking, book learning or ritual will bring you religion. Until that longing wakes up in you, you are no better off than an atheist.

Swamiji added another picture from a great sage. Imagine a thief in a room who learns that a huge pile of gold lies in the next room, with only a thin wall in between. Could he sleep? Could he eat? His whole mind would be fixed on that gold. If people truly believed that the source of all happiness and glory was right here, would they live the way they do, without even trying to reach God?

Once a person is truly convinced there is a far higher life than this one, and that the body and senses are nothing next to the endless joy of the Self, he becomes almost mad with longing until he finds it. That burning thirst, Swamiji said, is the real awakening of religion. Only when it arrives does a person begin to be religious.
learn: Saying you want something is easy; wanting it the way a drowning person wants air is different. Whether your goal is spiritual growth, a skill or a cause, check how strong your hunger actually is. Real intensity changes how you spend your days.
